title: How to Get More Roofing Leads in 2026
desc: How to get more roofing leads in 2026: Google, reviews, neighbour knocks, inspections, storm work and paid leads, with cost per job sums and scripts to copy.

blocks.h1: How to get more roofing leads, *without chasing every storm.*
blocks.lede: To get more roofing leads, make sure homeowners can find and trust you before the roof starts leaking: a complete Google Business Profile, steady reviews, a website with a page for each roofing service, and photos of local jobs. Then add the cheap, direct sources most roofers skip: the neighbours around every job, free roof inspections, gutter and maintenance work, and past customers. Use paid leads to fill gaps, and judge them by cost per signed job, not cost per lead.

blocks.html:
How do you get more roofing leads?

Roofing is different from most trades. People do not think about their roof until it leaks, a storm hits or they sell the house. When that moment comes, they want someone local and safe, fast. So the roofers who get the most leads do two things well: they are easy to find on the day of the problem, and they look like the obvious safe choice when the homeowner compares three names.

Here is the short list, in the order we would do it:

  1. Fix your Google Business Profile. Pick "Roofing contractor" as the main category, list every town you cover, and add photos of real local roofs every week.
  2. Get a review after every job. Roofs are big, scary purchases. Reviews that mention the suburb and the job type do a lot of selling for you.
  3. Build a page for each service. Roof repair, replacement, leak detection, flat roofs, gutters, storm damage. One page each, with photos and the areas you cover.
  4. Knock on the neighbours around every job. Your trucks and scaffolding are already the advert.
  5. Offer roof inspections and maintenance. Small jobs today become replacements later.
  6. Answer fast. A homeowner with water coming through the ceiling calls the next number if you do not pick up.
  7. Buy leads carefully. Paid platforms can fill a quiet month, but only if the sums work.

What do homeowners look for when choosing a roofer?

Read any homeowner thread after a hailstorm and the advice is the same. People in r/homeowners tell each other not to sign with whoever knocks first, and to call a local roofer that was in business well before the storm, check their reviews and get three quotes. That is good news for an established local roofer, as long as you can prove you are one.

Proof that you are local and safe looks like this:

  • A business address and phone number in the area, the same everywhere online
  • Reviews from named suburbs or towns, spread over months and years
  • Photos of finished roofs that a homeowner might recognise
  • Your licence, insurance and any manufacturer or trade body membership shown clearly
  • A website that has been there a while and lists the services you actually do

If a homeowner searches your name and finds a thin profile and no website, you look the same as the storm chaser in the rented truck. Our Google Business Profile checklist covers the profile part step by step.

Where do roofing leads come from without paying for them?

Google Maps and search

Most roofing searches are local: "roof repair near me", "roof leak repair [town]", "roofers in [suburb]". The map results are driven by your profile, your reviews and how close you are. The plain results below them are driven by your website. A roofer with one page that says "we do all roofing" competes badly with one that has a separate page for each service and each main area. See local SEO for trades for how it fits together.

The neighbours around every job

This is the cheapest lead source in roofing and most firms waste it. Houses on the same street are usually the same age, with roofs of the same age, so if one needs work, the next few often do too. Before you start, knock on the five houses either side and the five across the road, or drop a card. Keep it friendly and honest:

"Hi, I'm Sam from [business]. We're replacing the roof at number 14 this week, so you'll see our truck and some noise from Monday. Sorry in advance. While we're up there, if you'd like a free look at your roof, I can take a few photos and tell you honestly if it needs anything. Here's my card."

Then leave a sign out the front while you work, if local rules allow it, and send a short postcard or flyer to the street when the job is done with a photo of the finished roof.

Past customers and other trades

Every roof you have done has gutters, flashings and moss to deal with later. Keep a simple list of past customers with the address, job and date. Text them before your local storm or winter season to offer a check. Builders, plumbers, solar installers, painters, gutter cleaners, home inspectors and real estate agents all see roofs every week. Ask two or three of them to send you work and send work back.

Do free roof inspections bring in good leads?

Yes, when they are honest. A free inspection gets you on the roof, lets you take photos, and gives the homeowner a reason to trust you. The trap is the high pressure "you need a whole new roof" visit, which homeowners now expect and push back on. The inspections that turn into work look like this:

  1. Book a time and turn up on time.
  2. Take clear photos of every problem, plus wide shots that show the roof is generally fine where it is.
  3. Send a short written report the same day: what you found, what is urgent, what can wait a year or two, and a price for each.
  4. If the roof is fine, say so. That homeowner will remember you when it is not, and tell their neighbours.

A text to copy after the visit: "Hi Linda, thanks for having me today. Your report and photos are here: [link]. The only urgent item is the cracked flashing at the chimney, which I can fix for [price]. The rest of the roof has a few good years left. Any questions, just reply here."

How should you handle storm and insurance work?

After hail, wind or heavy rain, searches and calls jump. Storm work can fill your book for months, but it has rules and a reputation problem, so do it properly.

  • Be ready before the season. A storm damage page on your website, a "storm damage" post on your Google profile, and a plan for who answers the phone when it rings fifty times a day.
  • Help, do not pressure. Offer to photograph the damage and explain the next step. Let the homeowner deal with their insurer, and give them the photos and a clear quote.
  • Never offer to cover or waive a deductible. In the USA, a 2026 summary of state laws counts at least 23 states that bar contractors from paying, waiving or rebating an insurance deductible, or from promising to. In Texas it is a Class B misdemeanor under Business and Commerce Code section 27.02. Colorado has a similar rule for residential roofing.
  • Check door knocking rules. Many US towns require a solicitor permit, and some ban knocking after a set time. In the UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand, cold calling at the door is also covered by consumer law, with cooling off rights for contracts signed at home. Check your local rules before a canvassing day.
  • Look after the customers you already have first. A text to past customers in the storm area is worth more than a stranger's door.

Copy this for past customers after a storm: "Hi Mark, it's Sam from [business]. That storm hit [area] hard last night. If you've noticed any leaks or missing tiles, send me a photo and I'll prioritise you this week. Stay dry."

This guide is general information, not legal or financial advice.

Are paid roofing leads worth it?

They can be, as long as you measure cost per signed job, not cost per lead. The main paid options:

SourceHow it worksReported 2026 cost per lead (USA)
Shared marketplace leads (Angi, HomeAdvisor, Thumbtack)The same homeowner is often sent to three to five roofersRoughly $15 to $110, depending on the source and job type
Google Local Services AdsYou pay per lead, shown at the top with a Google Verified badgeOne tracking firm measured an average of $79 across 10 roofers in early 2026
Google Ads (search)You pay per click on your own adsThe same firm measured $124 per lead on non branded search
Exclusive lead vendorsA lead sent only to youRoughly $100 to $300

Shared leads look cheap, but close rates are low because you are racing other roofers to the same phone. One roofing industry guide this year works it through: a $60 shared lead that closes 6% of the time costs $1,000 per signed job, while a $120 lead that closes 25% of the time costs $480.

Here is the sum to run on your own numbers, for one month:

StepExample
Spend on the source$1,500
Leads received20 (so $75 a lead)
Inspections or quotes booked10
Jobs signed2
Cost per signed job$1,500 / 2 = $750
Average profit per job (after materials and labour)Your number here

If the cost per signed job is well below your profit per job, keep going. If not, cut it and put the time into reviews, neighbours and your website. In the UK, Checkatrade says it saw over 1.7 million roofing job searches on its site in 2025, and in Australia many roofers use hipages. Both can be worth it in the right area. Our guides on whether Checkatrade is worth it and Local Services Ads run the same sums for those platforms.

Why are you losing roofing leads you already have?

Many roofers do not have a lead problem. They have a follow up problem. The usual leaks:

  • Missed calls while on a roof. If you cannot answer, have a text go back within minutes: "Sorry I missed you, I'm on a roof. What's the address and what's going on? I'll call you back by [time]."
  • Slow quotes. A replacement quote that arrives a week later loses to the one that arrived the next morning.
  • No follow up. Send a friendly check two days after the quote and again a week later. Most people are busy, not saying no.
  • Quotes with no photos. Put the inspection photos in the quote. A homeowner who can see the problem understands the price.

Fixing these costs nothing and turns more of this month's enquiries into jobs.

Does this work the same in the UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand?

The basics are the same everywhere: a strong Google profile, reviews, a clear website and fast replies. The local details change:

  • USA: hail and hurricane seasons drive huge spikes, along with insurance work and the deductible rules above. Manufacturer certifications are often shown on websites as a trust signal.
  • UK: autumn and winter storms bring repair calls. Homeowners often check trade directories and look for trade body membership as well as Google reviews.
  • Canada: ice dams, snow load and a short summer replacement season. Book replacements early in spring and sell inspections before winter. HomeStars is the common directory.
  • Australia and New Zealand: storm seasons bring repair and restoration calls, and roof restoration and gutter guard work are common steady earners alongside full replacements.

Whichever country you are in, a website page for each service and each main area is what lets Google send you the right searches. See what a trade website needs.

blocks.title: Your checklist.
items: Set your Google Business Profile main category to roofing contractor and list every area you cover
Add photos of a real local roof to your profile every week
Ask every customer for a review on the day the job is finished
Build one website page for each roofing service and each main area
Knock or drop a card on 15 neighbouring houses before every job
Send a written report with photos the same day as every inspection
Set up an automatic text back for calls you miss while on a roof
Work out the cost per signed job for every paid lead source each month

items.q: What is the best way to get roofing leads?
items.a: For most local roofers, a complete Google Business Profile with steady reviews and local photos, a website with a page for each service, and knocking on neighbours around every job bring the best leads for the least money. Paid sources can top them up.

items.q: How much do roofing leads cost in 2026?
items.a: Reported US prices run from about $15 for some shared marketplace leads to $300 for exclusive leads, with Google Local Services Ads measured at around $79 a lead in one 2026 study. What matters is the cost per signed job, which depends on your close rate.

items.q: Is door knocking still worth it for roofers?
items.a: Knocking on the neighbours around a job you are already doing works well because your work is right there. Cold knocking after storms is harder, as many homeowners distrust it, and many towns require a permit.

items.q: How do roofers get leads in the off season?
items.a: Sell inspections, gutter cleaning, moss removal and maintenance, text past customers before storm or winter season, and book replacements early for spring. Small jobs keep you visible and turn into replacements later.

items.q: Are Angi leads worth it for roofers?
items.a: They can fill gaps in some areas, but shared leads go to several roofers, so close rates are low. Track cost per signed job for a month or two before deciding.

items.q: Can roofers offer to cover a customer's deductible?
items.a: In many US states, including Texas and Colorado, it is illegal for a roofer to pay, waive or rebate a deductible or to promise to. Check the rules in your state.
